St Kilda has successfully had Lance Collard's ban for a homophobic slur reduced at the appeals board.

The appeals board deemed the AFL Tribunal's initial sanction of nine weeks, two suspended, was "crippling" for Collard's career.

Collard's suspension was reduced to four weeks, two suspended.

St Kilda forward Lance Collard's ban for a homophobic slur has been reduced from nine weeks to four after an appeal hearing determined the original sanction was "crippling".

In a hearing which lasted two hours , Collard's defence was able to successfully argue that the AFL's original sanction over an incident in the VFL on March 27 was manifestly excessive.

The AFL has accepted the appeals board's decision and considers the matter closed.

The damage is already done irregardless of the length of the sanction handed down to Lance Collard, writes Marnie Vinall.

"It is to the credit of the AFL and the tribunal that its efforts to eliminate [homophobic abuse] appear to be succeeding," said the chairman of the appeals board, Will Houghton KC.

"However, that cannot be at the price of imposing what this board considers to be a crippling penalty on the appellant in this case.

"We describe it as crippling because there was evidence before the tribunal in the sanction in both hearings that a penalty of this extent would finish him off as a player of professional football.

"Firstly, his previous misconduct in 2024 was more serious and probably far more serious than the present affairs."

The appeals board threw out St Kilda's assertion that the AFL had incorrectly charged Collard under Rule 2.3(a) for conduct unbecoming to the league instead of using Rule 35, the Peek Rule, which is used to address vilification.

"The comment found to have been made by Collard is disgraceful in the view of the appeal board and clearly homophobic," Houghton said.

"A comment like that has no place on the football field. It clearly comes within rule 2.3(a).

"There is no doubt in the appeal board's view that the offending comment was conduct unbecoming."

Collard has a chance to represent St Kilda at the AFL level this season for the first time since round 24 last year. ( Getty Images: Robert Cianflone )

The appeals board also took into account Collard's age, his background and the fact that the target of the slur, Frankston's Darby Hipwell, had previously told the tribunal he was not offended by the slur.

St Kilda once again referred to instances of Zak Butters, Dale Thomas and Dane Rampe being fined rather than suspended for using abusive language against officials as a part of its argument.

The Saints also used an incident involving Alastair Clarkson from 2024 to argue the initial suspension handed down to Collard was excessive.

The Collard verdict is another loss to the AFL Tribunal after an umpire abuse charge against Zak Butters was thrown out. ( ABC News: Briana Fiore )

On that occasion, Clarkson was fined $20,000 and handed an entirely suspended two-match ban over using a homophobic slur against two St Kilda players during a pre-season contest.

St Kilda referenced the Clarkson sanction and asked for Collard to be handed either an entirely financial sanction or a sanction of four weeks and was ultimately successful.

The reduction of Collard's suspension brings to an end another drawn-out tribunal process after Butters had his umpire-abuse charge thrown out.

The AFL ultimately issued an apology over a tribunal panel member's decision to disconnect from the initial hearing then continue listening while driving.

Last week, St Kilda coach Ross Lyon labelled the AFL's tribunal process a "firestorm", saying it put unnecessary stress on the individuals involved.

Topic: War

Iranian state TV broadcasts video of the seizure of two ships by the IRGC. ( Reuters: IRIB )

Ten days ago Donald Trump ordered US Navy warships to sail into the Gulf of Oman and announced the United States was blockading Iranian ports and shutting down the regime's oil trade.

Since then, a battle of the blockades has ensued as Iran has backflipped on what to do with the Strait of Hormuz.

As different directives were announced, some ships have crossed the strait while others have been turned around.

And despite the US announcing ships from all Iranian ports were under blockade, data shows several ships likely linked to Iran have made it through.

Some ships have been seized by US forces, while others have been fired upon by Iran and, most recently, boarded by the regime's revolutionary guards.

This is all while both sides maintain there is a ceasefire in place and as a second round of peace talks lingers.

On Wednesday, local time, Iran fired upon three ships and seized two of them in the Strait of Hormuz. It was the first time in the war Iran had seized ships.

This is after the US had seized both the Iranian flagged Touska as it tried to enter the Persian Gulf, and a vessel called Tifani as it made its way through the Indian Ocean, reportedly laden with Iranian oil .

Both sides say they have a level of control over the strait.

The US naval blockade to traffic from Iranian ports is in spite of the tenuous ceasefire brokered weeks ago.

Meanwhile Iran, now believed to be increasingly controlled by its military apparatus, appears to be flexing its remaining military might over the body of water that has proven to be its biggest leverage in the war against it.

To understand both the blockade and the traffic that is moving across the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, it's important to look at the affiliations of the vessels, where they are departing from and their destination.

It is only vessels interacting with Iranian ports that have been under US blockade, according to US Central Command.

This applied not just to Iranian flagged ships, but "vessels of all nations" entering or departing Iranian ports and coastal areas, CENTCOM said.

Typically, that would include oil going to Iran's biggest customers, including China and Pakistan, but ships use a variety of tactics to obscure their identity.

On April 13 when the announcement was made, CENTCOM said its forces would not "impede freedom of navigation for vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz to and from non-Iranian ports."

Early in the blockade, the US military sent a note to seafarers saying any vessel entering or departing the blockaded area without authorisation was "subject to interception, diversion, and capture," according to Reuters.

It also appears as if the US blockade is turning back sanctioned vessels.

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has remained at an effective standstill in the 24 hours since Iran conditionally lifted its blockade on the critical shipping lane, amid a fragile ceasefire with the US and Israel.

Kpler Marine Traffic data shows several ships have made it through the strait since the start of the blockade, and that would be in line with the conditions published by CENTCOM, providing they are not entering or departing Iranian ports.

Looking at available tracking data since 12pm AEST on April 13 — when the blockade came into effect — and up until Sunday night, there had been 62 tankers as well as cargo and container bulk carriers that had been tracked as crossing the Strait of Hormuz.

But it is what happens afterwards that is perhaps most important.

Some of those ships are attempting to cross into the Persian Gulf, others are trying to escape in the opposite direction, past the blockade and out into the Arabian and Indian seas, typically laden with cargo, oil or LPG.

Among the ships that appear to have made it beyond the US blockade to the Arabian and Indian seas are several with destinations including India, South Korea and Taiwan.

Early Thursday morning the US said nearly 30 ships had been turned around as part of its blockade against Iran .

But according to available Kpler tracking data, four vessels believed to be either Iranian flagged or having departed from an Iranian port have made it across the Strait of Hormuz and out of the region since the blockade began.

One Iranian flagged ship the ABC has verified as crossing the strait after the blockade started shows no tracking path until it emerges from the blockaded area.

It continues on to Singapore and then further into the South China Sea.

An apparently sanctioned ship attempted to cross the strait but had to turn around, likely due to the US blockade. ( Supplied: Kpler )

It is worth noting, ship tracking data only records vessels that move with their transponders turned on. Iran and some of its customers have long been running shadow fleets where ships move without broadcasting accurate tracking data or any at all.

Before the war around 130 vessels crossed the strait each day, a figure that has plummeted to just a handful a day since fighting began.

Choking traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, where 20 per cent of the world's oil trade typically moves through, has been a strategic success for Iran in this war, inflicting economic pain across US and global markets and ratcheting up political pressure on Mr Trump.

But it has reportedly also become a point of contention inside Iran.

Analysts have said that when the US bombed Iran last year in the so-called 12-day war, some in the regime believed it was a misstep to not move on the Strait of Hormuz then.

Eight months later the regime did not hesitate again.

By moving so much of the war into the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf, Tehran has hit its adversaries where it hurts the most and analysts warn that while the United States military is mighty, history shows in asymmetrical warfare, the lesser power can win the day.

Shortly after the war broke out at the end of February, IRGC forces active in the strait began to broadcast a message to vessels in the area: "No ship is allowed to pass the Strait of Hormuz."

Among the messages from Washington, Mr Trump has said the opening of the strait was not a priority of the US or an objective of the war effort.

But then he has also told the Iranians: "Open the F**kin' Strait, you crazy bastards."

When the US announced the blockade, in theory it only shut down traffic from Iranian ports, but still the flow of ships from other ports was still massively restrained compared to pre-war levels.

Then the situation became even more confusing.

On the morning of April 17 a 10-day truce between Israel and Lebanon came into effect which sparked hope Iran might lift its foot off the neck of global shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran had said ending Israel's war with Hezbollah was one of its key demands.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi then announced the Strait of Hormuz would be opened to commercial traffic, but this day turned out to be a particularly chaotic day for vessels in the area.

After announcing the strait open Iran clarified ships would still need to seek permission to make the crossing.

Iran has effectively blocked the only way out of the Persian Gulf, leaving about 3,000 ships stranded. But two zombie ships appear to have sailed in and out of the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz.

Across the 24-hour period from 10am AEST Saturday, the number of ships trying to cross the Strait of Hormuz jumped.

At least 24 tankers, as well as cargo and container bulk carriers, made it across the strait in either direction, according to Kpler marine traffic data.

From voyage information it appears as if at least nine of those ships crossed the Strait of Hormuz to sail out of the Gulf of Oman and onto onward journeys.

Among the others were ships crossing into the Persian Gulf, those that dropped off tracking or appear to have been turned back.

But the following day the IRGC insisted the Strait of Hormuz was closed, jolting global markets once again while also putting on full display the power struggle inside Iran.

"The confidence from commercial shipping that looked like it was safe to transit evaporated quickly," said senior maritime intelligence analyst with Windward, Michelle Wiese Bockmann.

Speaking of the impact of the Iranian announcements, Ms Bockmann said: "We are not even back to square one."

She said the shipping industry was in a worse position than before the strait was opened and then closed again, "because at least back then you saw under the permission-based system some vessels which rerouted through Iranian waters."

The White House is working hard to insist its ceasefire with Iran is holding. This is while Iran has not yet committed to putting its delegation on a plane to Islamabad for another round of peace talks — something expected to be key in reaching an actual deal.

Days ago, Tehran left US Vice President JD Vance hanging and Air Force Two fuelled and ready to depart for the Pakistani capital before hopes of talks evaporated.

Internal ructions in Iran's regime may be playing a role, with Mr Trump posting on Truth Social the regime was "seriously fractured" and "we have been asked to hold our attack on the country of Iran until such time as their leaders and representatives can come up with a unified proposal".

He then extended the ceasefire indefinitely.

These are the key moments that lead up to a two-week ceasefire agreement between the US and Iran, and what is on the table to permanently end the fighting.

US press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in a recent interview on Fox News that since the ships seized by Iran were not US or Israeli vessels the move was not a violation of the ceasefire. She called it an act of "piracy".

However, Iran has slammed the US over their blockade.

Iran's parliament speaker and lead negotiator Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf told Mr Trump: "You did not achieve your goals through military aggression, and you will not achieve them by bullying either."

Iranian military might is again being flexed across the Strait of Hormuz while US warships blockade regime oil leaving its ports just to the west in the Gulf of Oman.

Washington appears to be waiting for the opportunity to make a deal while Tehran's political and military elite are yet to agree on whether it still wants one.

And for the thousands of sailors on ships in the Persian Gulf, their third month of being stranded approaches.
